Why Cities Are Rethinking the Night Bus

By Lena Okafor · Updated March 3, 2026 · 7 min read

For most of the twentieth century, the night bus was an afterthought: a skeleton service for shift workers, students, and anyone who had missed the last train. Transit agencies treated it as a cost to be minimized rather than a network to be designed.

That is starting to change. Over the past five years, a growing number of cities have rebuilt their overnight networks from scratch, and the results have surprised even the planners who championed them.

The hidden ridership

When Barcelona redesigned its NitBus routes in 2022, officials expected modest gains. Instead, overnight ridership rose by 38 percent within eighteen months. Most of the new riders were not revellers but workers: cleaners, nurses, bakers, and warehouse staff whose shifts begin or end while the city sleeps.

Advertisement

"We had been designing for the people we imagined," said Marta Vidal, who led the redesign. "Once we looked at the data, it was obvious we had been ignoring the people who actually needed us."

The night network is not a smaller version of the day network. It has its own geography.

What changed

The cities that have succeeded share a few common choices:

  • Frequent, simple trunk routes instead of dozens of meandering lines.
  • Timed transfers at a small number of well-lit hubs.
  • Real-time arrival information at every stop, not just the busy ones.

None of these ideas is new. What is new is the willingness to fund them. In Vienna, Seoul, and Montreal, overnight service now receives a dedicated budget line rather than whatever is left over after daytime operations.

Safety as a design input

Riders consistently rank personal safety above speed. Agencies that added staffed hubs, better lighting, and request stops for women travelling alone saw the largest increases in first-time riders, according to a 2025 survey by the International Association of Public Transport.

Dr. Samuel Reyes, a transport researcher at U.C.L.A., cautions against reading too much into early numbers. "It's easy to grow from a low base," he said. "The question is whether cities keep funding these networks once the press releases stop."

The road ahead

For now, the momentum is real. Dozens of mid-sized cities are studying the Barcelona model, and several national governments have begun to tie transit funding to overnight service levels. The night bus, long the forgotten child of public transport, may finally be getting its moment.
